excerpts.author: ethdreamer
excerpts.content:
The signature aggregation is the separate **Prove one** column. That produces a proof for one committee.

For the rows with 16 committees per slot:
- **Round 1:** merge 16 committee proofs into one proof, P1.
- **Round 2:** merge P1 with 15 more committee proofs from an older slot, producing P2.
- **Round 3:** merge P2 with 15 more committee proofs from another older slot.

So all three numbered rounds are recursive merges. Each later round reuses the previous result and adds more votes; it isn't just merging the same votes again. The extra proofs are already prepared before we start timing the merges.

excerpts.author: ethdreamer
excerpts.content:
Yes, you've got the earliest inclusion slots right. The key is that it's a **minimum delay**, not a one-slot opportunity: the block at N can include votes from N-2 **and older votes that are still eligible**.

Missed blocks are one reason older votes might be left over, but not the only one. A block can be produced without including every vote, or an aggregate can arrive too late for that proposer.

Extra merge rounds can also add a late or more complete aggregate for N-2 itself.

Our benchmark deliberately adds older, not-yet-included votes in rounds 2 and 3 to measure that heavier workload. It does **not** mean every block needs three rounds. If the first merge covers all the useful votes you have, you're done.

excerpts.author: terencechain
excerpts.content:
my naive algorithm is like this:

If I haven't seen a block 3s into a slot, I assume that slot will be skipped or reorged. So for that same slot, I merge its aggregate attestations into one proof at around the 9s

Ex: say I'm proposing at N+2 and we're in slot N-2. I build and keep a proof for the N-2 votes. If a proposer before me (N or N+1) ends up including attestations that cover the same bitfield, I discard the proof
